sources: University of California IPM, Pantry Pests (Pest Notes 7452): the Indian meal moth is the most common moth pest of stored food in homes; adults have reddish-brown or copper outer wings with a pale grey-cream base; larvae feed on grains, cereals, flour, dried fruit, nuts, pet food, birdseed and chocolate, and leave silk webbing in the food; mature larvae often leave the food to pupate and may be found on walls and ceilings; adult moths do not feed on stored products; some pantry pests can chew through thin plastic bags and cardboard, so store food in glass, metal or heavy plastic containers with tight lids; freezing infested or new products (0 F for about 4 days) kills all stages; https://ipm.ucanr.edu/PMG/PESTNOTES/pn7452.html

University of Florida Featured Creatures, Indian meal moth (Plodia interpunctella): the common name comes from an early report of the larvae feeding on Indian meal, a historical name for cornmeal; females lay roughly 60 to 400 eggs; https://entnemdept.ufl.edu/creatures/urban/stored/indian_meal_moth.htm

beats.say: Number eleven. The pantry moth. Copper wing tips, and pale shoulders.
The grown up moth doesn't eat your food at all. But mom lays hundreds of eggs, right in it.
The babies eat cereal, flour, nuts, dried fruit, even pet food and chocolate.
And they leave sticky silk webs in it. So that clumpy cereal? Check it for webs.
Thin plastic bags won't stop them. They chew right through, and through cardboard too.
Pantry moth. D tier. Bad news for your cereal.
